outages.cause: Rolling and emergency blackouts after Russian attacks on energy infrastructure, including a large-scale attack on Nov 20, further strikes reported on subsequent days, including overnight and on the morning of Wednesday, Nov 25, additional Wednesday afternoon strikes in several regions, and further strikes that Ukrenergo said took place during Thursday, Nov 26. Ukrenergo, as reported by UNIAN at 9:37 p.m. Friday, Nov 27, said that on Saturday, Nov 28, consumption restrictions would be applied in some regions of Ukraine: hourly outage schedules of 1 to 3 queues for all categories of consumers, and capacity-limitation schedules for industry. The same UNIAN report, citing Ukrenergo, said a difficult electricity-supply situation remained in Zaporizhzhia and Dnipropetrovsk regions, where emergency outages continued to be applied because of damage to energy infrastructure from Russian shelling, and that energy workers had managed to normalize the electricity-supply situation in Kherson region. DTEK, as reported by Ukrinform at 2:37 p.m. Friday, Nov 27, said that as of 2:20 p.m. Friday, emergency outages had been introduced on Ukrenergo's command in Buchanskyi, Obukhivskyi, and Fastivskyi districts of Kyiv region, and reminded that during emergency outages the schedules do not apply. Ukrenergo, as reported by Korrespondent at 12:17 p.m. Friday, Nov 27, and earlier by Ukrinform at 11:56 a.m. Friday, said that as a result of enemy shelling, emergency outages were in effect in Dnipropetrovsk and Zaporizhzhia regions, that repair crews were working wherever it was safe, though repeated attacks on energy facilities and lines already restored after earlier shelling were complicating the work, and that a return to hourly outage schedules would take place as soon as the situation in the power system allowed. Ukrenergo, as reported by Ukrinform at 10:42 a.m. Friday, Nov 27, said that during the previous day the enemy had again struck key energy facilities and distribution networks, and that as of Friday morning there were de-energized consumers in Dnipropetrovsk, Zaporizhzhia, Kirovohrad, Sumy, Kharkiv, and Kherson regions, with the situation remaining difficult in Dnipropetrovsk and Kherson regions, where a significant portion of consumers had been de-energized, and with emergency outages being applied in Dnipropetrovsk region as of 10:20 a.m. Friday. That Friday morning list of six regions with de-energized consumers differed from Thursday morning's seven-region list, which had named Dnipropetrovsk, Zhytomyr, Zaporizhzhia, Mykolaiv, Odesa, Kharkiv, and Chernihiv, and had not named Kirovohrad, Sumy, or Kherson. Suspilne, citing Ukrenergo on Friday morning, said that because of damage to energy infrastructure, restrictions would be in effect until the end of the day in some regions: capacity-limitation schedules for industry, and hourly outage schedules of 0.5 to 3.5 queues for all categories of consumers. Ukrenergo, as reported Thursday evening by RBC-Ukraine at 8:40 p.m. Thursday, Nov 26, had already said that on Friday, Nov 27, planned restrictions would be in effect throughout the day in some regions because of the consequences of attacks on the power system. The Energy Ministry, as reported in Wednesday morning accounts, and the IAEA, as reported by TASS citing an IAEA press-service statement, had said the temporarily occupied Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant had lost its external power supply and switched to diesel generators. The IAEA, in Update 377 dated Nov 26, 2026, said the plant's connection to its sole remaining external power line, the 330 kV Ferosplavna-1 line, was lost on Nov 25 at 5:28 a.m. local time, reportedly due to military activity, that this was the 28th time during the conflict that ZNPP was relying on emergency diesel generators, and that the IAEA was engaging with the Russian Federation and Ukraine on arrangements for a ninth localized ceasefire to facilitate repair of the line. ZNPP communications director Yevgenia Yashina, as reported by TASS on Nov 26 from Melitopol, said that as of the morning of Nov 26 the Ferrosplavnaya-1 line remained disconnected, that the location of the malfunction had been identified, and that it was still too early to say when electricity would be restored.
outages.affected: Ukrenergo, as reported by UNIAN at 9:37 p.m. Friday, Nov 27 (1:37 p.m. CT), said that on Saturday, Nov 28, consumption restrictions would be applied in some regions of Ukraine: hourly outage schedules of 1 to 3 queues for all categories of consumers, which UNIAN said means from 4 to 12 hours without electricity, and capacity-limitation schedules for industry. The same UNIAN report, citing Ukrenergo, said a difficult electricity-supply situation remained in Zaporizhzhia and Dnipropetrovsk regions, where emergency outages continued to be applied because of damage to energy infrastructure from Russian shelling, and that energy workers had managed to normalize the electricity-supply situation in Kherson region. Censor.NET, in a report dated 7:42 p.m. Friday, Nov 27 (11:42 a.m. CT), and UNN, in a report dated 5:41 p.m. Friday, Nov 27 (9:41 a.m. CT if Kyiv time), had earlier likewise reported Ukrenergo's Saturday schedules of 1 to 3 queues around the clock in some regions. DTEK, as reported by Ukrinform at 2:37 p.m. Friday, Nov 27 (6:37 a.m. CT), said that as of 2:20 p.m. Friday (6:20 a.m. CT), emergency outages had been introduced on Ukrenergo's command in Buchanskyi, Obukhivskyi, and Fastivskyi districts of Kyiv region, and reminded that during emergency outages the schedules do not apply. Ukrinform also recalled that emergency outages had been introduced on Friday morning in Dnipropetrovsk and Zaporizhzhia regions. Ukrenergo, as reported by Korrespondent at 12:17 p.m. Friday, Nov 27 (4:17 a.m. CT), and by Ukrinform at 11:56 a.m. Friday (3:56 a.m. CT), said that as of 11:40 a.m. Friday emergency outages were in effect in Dnipropetrovsk and Zaporizhzhia regions as a result of enemy shelling, that repair crews were working wherever it was safe, and that a return to hourly outage schedules would take place as soon as the situation in the power system allowed. Ukrenergo, as reported by Ukrinform at 10:42 a.m. Friday, Nov 27 (2:42 a.m. CT), said that as of Friday morning, as a result of Russian attacks on key energy facilities and distribution networks during the previous day, there were de-energized consumers in Dnipropetrovsk, Zaporizhzhia, Kirovohrad, Sumy, Kharkiv, and Kherson regions, that the situation remained difficult in Dnipropetrovsk and Kherson regions, where a significant portion of consumers had been de-energized, and that as of 10:20 a.m. Friday emergency outages were being applied in Dnipropetrovsk region. Suspilne, in a report published at 10:38 a.m. Friday, Nov 27 (2:38 a.m. CT), citing Ukrenergo, named the same six regions, said the most difficult situation was in Dnipropetrovsk and Kherson regions, and said that because of damage to energy infrastructure, restrictions would be in effect until the end of the day in some regions: capacity-limitation schedules for industry, and hourly outage schedules of 0.5 to 3.5 queues for all categories of consumers. Apostrophe, in a report published at 11:57 a.m. Friday, Nov 27 (3:57 a.m. CT), said First Deputy Energy Minister Artem Nekrasov, in a briefing on the power-system situation as of Nov 27, said that as a result of Russian strikes on energy infrastructure, some consumers in six regions of Ukraine remained without electricity, that the most difficult situation was in Dnipropetrovsk and Kherson regions, and that emergency outages were additionally being applied in Dnipropetrovsk region. OBOZ.UA, in a report published at 11:49 a.m. Friday, Nov 27, and updated at 1:09 p.m. Friday (5:09 a.m. CT), citing Ukrenergo and the Ministry of Energy, said that after 11:30 a.m. Friday emergency outages had begun in Dnipropetrovsk and Zaporizhzhia regions, where hourly schedules were not in effect, and wrote that in some regions, including Kharkiv region, outages were reaching 13 to 15 hours over a 24-hour period. Ukrenergo, as reported by RBC-Ukraine at 8:40 p.m. Thursday, Nov 26 (12:40 p.m. CT), had said that on Friday, Nov 27, planned consumption restrictions would be in effect throughout the day in some regions of Ukraine: capacity-limitation schedules for industry, and hourly outage schedules of 0.5 to 3.5 queues for all other categories of consumers. The IAEA, in Update 377 dated Nov 26, 2026, said the Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant's connection to its sole remaining external power line, the 330 kV Ferosplavna-1 line, was lost on Nov 25 at 5:28 a.m. local time, reportedly due to military activity, that this was the 28th time during the conflict that ZNPP was relying on emergency diesel generators, that the IAEA was engaging with both sides on arrangements for a ninth localized ceasefire to facilitate repair of the line, and that the IAEA estimated the plant had sufficient diesel fuel to maintain its then-current configuration of two operating emergency diesel generators for more than ten days. TASS, in a Nov 26 report from Melitopol, quoted ZNPP communications director Yevgenia Yashina as saying that as of the morning of Nov 26, the Ferrosplavnaya-1 line remained disconnected, that the location of the malfunction had been identified, and that it was still too early to say when electricity would be restored. No official nationwide customer count was found as of 6:00 PM CT Friday, Nov 27 (2:00 a.m. Saturday, Nov 28, EET), and no later official confirmation that ZNPP external power had been restored was found.

outages.place: Odesa, including Prymorskyi and Peresypskyi districts, and parts of Odesa and Bolhrad districts
outages.cause: Repeated Russian attacks on high-voltage transmission networks and other energy facilities critical to the region, including a strike on a DTEK Odeski Elektromerezhi energy facility on the morning of Nov 20, further damage reported over Nov 24-25, and a massive strike-drone attack on Odesa and its suburbs on the afternoon of Wednesday, Nov 25. Odesa regional governor Oleh Kiper, as reported by Ukrinform at 12:43 p.m. Wednesday, Nov 25, said that over the past day Russian attacks had again damaged energy equipment in Odesa region. Kiper, as reported later Wednesday by Censor.NET at 1:59 p.m. and by Kyiv Post, said Russian forces had launched a massive attack with strike drones against Odesa and its suburbs, targeting civilian and energy infrastructure. DTEK Odeski Elektromerezhi, as reported Wednesday morning by Odessa Life in an update at 7:54 a.m., said stabilization outages would be applied in Odesa and Odesa region on Wednesday, Nov 25, on Ukrenergo's command, and that schedules could be adjusted if Ukrenergo's commands changed. The same Odessa Life report, citing the company, also said urgent equipment repairs in Odesa's Peresypskyi district would leave that area without electricity from 8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. Wednesday, as previously announced. On Thursday, Nov 26, DTEK Odeski Elektromerezhi, as reported by Odessa Life, said stabilization outages would apply in Odesa and Odesa region to all 12 of the company's schedule groups because of the consequences of attacks on the energy system. Ukrenergo, as reported by Ukrinform at 11:00 a.m. Thursday, Nov 26, listed Odesa region among seven regions with de-energized consumers as of Thursday morning On Friday, Nov 27, DTEK Odeski Elektromerezhi, as reported by Odessa Life at 10:52 p.m. Thursday, Nov 26, said stabilization outages would again apply in Odesa and Odesa region to all 12 of the company's schedule groups because of the consequences of attacks on the energy system. Odessa Life, in a report published at 9:30 p.m. Friday, Nov 27, said stabilization outages would again apply in Odesa and Odesa region on Saturday, Nov 28, to all 12 of the company's schedule groups.
outages.affected: Odessa Life, in a report published at 9:30 p.m. Friday, Nov 27 (1:30 p.m. CT), said that on Saturday, Nov 28, stabilization outage schedules would continue to apply in Odesa and Odesa region to all 12 DTEK Odeski Elektromerezhi consumer groups, that schedules could change during the day depending on Ukrenergo's commands, and that customers could check times for their address on the DTEK website and in the company's Viber and Telegram channels. That report did not publish a full table of Saturday group hours. Novyny.LIVE, in a report published at 9:20 a.m. Friday, Nov 27 (1:20 a.m. CT), citing DTEK, said stabilization outage schedules were in effect in Odesa and Odesa region on Friday, Nov 27, after specialists had managed to stabilize the power system following a large-scale de-energization, that the restrictions applied to all consumer groups, and that schedules could change depending on the situation in the power system. The same report, citing DTEK, published these Friday group times: group 1.1, 8:00 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. and 6:30 p.m. to 10:30 p.m.; group 1.2, 8:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. and 6:30 p.m. to 10:30 p.m.; group 2.1, 8:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m., 2:00 p.m. to 3:30 p.m., and 6:30 p.m. to 10:30 p.m.; group 2.2, 8:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. and 6:30 p.m. to 10:30 p.m.; groups 3.1, 11:30 a.m. to 7:00 p.m.; group 3.2, 11:30 a.m. to 7:00 p.m. and 10:00 p.m. to 12:00 a.m.; groups 4.1 and 4.2, 11:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. and 10:00 p.m. to 12:00 a.m.; group 5.1, 6:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. and 3:00 p.m. to 7:00 p.m.; group 5.2, 6:00 a.m. to 8:30 a.m. and 3:00 p.m. to 7:00 p.m.; group 6.1, 6:00 a.m. to 8:30 a.m. and 3:00 p.m. to 10:30 p.m.; and group 6.2, 6:00 a.m. to 8:30 a.m. and 3:00 p.m. to 8:00 p.m. The same report said that on Friday, Nov 27, from 9:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m., energy workers would carry out urgent equipment repairs and that during that time electricity would be unavailable in part of Izmail district of Odesa region, with the period possibly extended if an air-raid alert was declared. Odessa Life, in a report published at 10:52 p.m. Thursday, Nov 26 (2:52 p.m. CT), had already said Friday stabilization outages in Odesa and Odesa region would apply to all 12 DTEK Odeski Elektromerezhi schedule groups, and that schedules could change on Ukrenergo's commands. Odesa region was named in Ukrenergo's Thursday morning list of regions with de-energized consumers, and was not named in Ukrenergo's Friday morning six-region list. No official customer count for Odesa or Odesa region was found as of 6:00 PM CT Friday, Nov 27 (2:00 a.m. Saturday, Nov 28, EET), and no official statement was found that Saturday's DTEK stabilization-outage schedules in Odesa and Odesa region had been cancelled.

outages.place: Dnipro and parts of Dnipropetrovsk region, including Dniprovskyi, Samarivskyi, Synelnykivskyi, and Pavlohradskyi districts
outages.cause: Russian attacks on energy facilities in Dnipropetrovsk region, including strikes on Nov 24 and overnight into Nov 25, a Wednesday, Nov 25, attack on one of DTEK's thermal power plants, a later Wednesday attack that DTEK said damaged main power grids, and further strikes that Ukrenergo said took place during Thursday, Nov 26. Ukrenergo, as reported by Ukrinform at 10:42 a.m. Friday, Nov 27, said a significant portion of consumers in Dnipropetrovsk region had been de-energized as a result of Russian attacks, and that as of 10:20 a.m. Friday emergency outages were being applied in the region. Ukrenergo, as reported by Ukrinform at 11:56 a.m. Friday, said that as of 11:40 a.m. Friday emergency outages were in effect in Dnipropetrovsk and Zaporizhzhia regions as a result of enemy shelling, and that a return to hourly outage schedules would take place as soon as the situation in the power system allowed. Dniprovska poradnytsia, in a report published at 10:22 a.m. Friday, Nov 27, citing DTEK, said emergency outages were in effect in Dnipro and in the Dniprovskyi, Pavlohradskyi, Synelnykivskyi, and Samarivskyi districts, and that schedules were also not in effect for Central Energy Company (TSEK) customers in Dnipro and Pavlohrad. Ukrenergo, as reported by UNIAN at 9:37 p.m. Friday, Nov 27, said emergency outages continued to be applied in Dnipropetrovsk region because of damage to energy infrastructure from Russian shelling.
outages.affected: Ukrenergo, as reported by UNIAN at 9:37 p.m. Friday, Nov 27 (1:37 p.m. CT), said a difficult electricity-supply situation remained in Zaporizhzhia and Dnipropetrovsk regions and that emergency outages continued to be applied in both regions because of damage to energy infrastructure from Russian shelling. Ukrenergo, as reported by Ukrinform at 10:42 a.m. Friday, Nov 27 (2:42 a.m. CT), had said the situation remained difficult in Dnipropetrovsk and Kherson regions, where a significant portion of consumers had been de-energized as a result of Russian attacks, and that as of 10:20 a.m. Friday emergency outages were being applied in Dnipropetrovsk region. Ukrenergo, as reported by Ukrinform at 11:56 a.m. Friday, Nov 27 (3:56 a.m. CT), said that as of 11:40 a.m. Friday emergency outages were in effect in Dnipropetrovsk and Zaporizhzhia regions as a result of enemy shelling, and that a return to hourly outage schedules would take place as soon as the situation in the power system allowed. Dniprovska poradnytsia, in a report published at 10:22 a.m. Friday, Nov 27 (2:22 a.m. CT), citing DTEK, said emergency outages were in effect in Dnipro and in the Dniprovskyi, Pavlohradskyi, Synelnykivskyi, and Samarivskyi districts, that schedules were not in effect there, and that schedules were also not in effect for Central Energy Company (TSEK) customers in Dnipro and Pavlohrad. Kamianskyi district, which DTEK had included in Thursday morning's emergency-outage list, was not named in that Friday morning DTEK account; Synelnykivskyi district, which had been named on Wednesday and was not named on Thursday morning, was again named on Friday. DTEK, as reported by Dnepr.info at 7:35 a.m. Thursday, Nov 26 (11:35 p.m. CT Wednesday, Nov 25), had said that on Thursday emergency outages were in effect in Dnipro and in the Dniprovskyi, Samarivskyi, Kamianskyi, and Pavlohradskyi districts, where schedules were not in effect, and that stabilization outages continued in the rest of the region. Ukrenergo, as reported by Korrespondent at 12:17 p.m. Friday, Nov 27 (4:17 a.m. CT), again said emergency outages were in effect in Dnipropetrovsk and Zaporizhzhia regions as a result of enemy shelling, and that a return to hourly schedules would take place as soon as the situation in the power system allowed. No official customer count for Dnipro or Dnipropetrovsk region was found as of 6:00 PM CT Friday, Nov 27 (2:00 a.m. Saturday, Nov 28, EET), and no later official statement was found that the emergency outages in Dnipropetrovsk region had ended.

outages.place: Kurdistan Region, including Erbil, Sulaymaniyah, Duhok, Bazian, and Chamchamal
outages.cause: Suspected drone attack on the Khor Mor gas field on the night of Nov 8, 2026, which halted gas production that supplies much of the region's electricity generation. Dana Gas, the field's operator, later said the facility had sustained significant damage and could produce no gas
outages.affected: 964media, in a report dated 11:18 p.m. Friday, Nov 27, 2026 (2:18 p.m. CT if Iraq time), citing an unnamed technical source familiar with restart work at the Khor Mor field who asked not to be named because he was not authorized to speak, said the field was expected to return to operation on Sunday, Nov 29, 2026, but at only one-third of its previous capacity. The source told 964media that work was scheduled to begin Sunday on the KM250 section, with a production capacity of 250 million cubic feet of gas a day; that the attacked KM400 section, which had a daily production capacity of 500 million cubic feet, had not yet had any maintenance work; and that repairing the attacked section, if work on it began, would take at least four to five months before it could start production. The same source said that of the 250 million cubic feet from the KM250 section, 150 million cubic feet had previously gone to consumption inside the Kurdistan Region and 100 million to electricity in Iraq, that it was not yet clear whether, once work resumed, the Iraqi government would allow the entire 250 million cubic feet to go to the Kurdistan Region, and that if the entire 250 million cubic feet were allocated to the Kurdistan Region, electricity supply there could rise to about 12 hours a day. The report said Khor Mor had produced 750 million cubic feet of gas a day before the attack, so 250 million cubic feet would equal one-third of its previous capacity, and that after the Nov 8 drone attack electricity supply in the Kurdistan Region had fallen from 24 hours a day to between 6 and 8 hours. Those statements were from an unnamed technical source and were not an official confirmation from Dana Gas or from the Kurdistan Region's electricity ministry that production had already resumed or that a Sunday restart was guaranteed. The New Region, in a Nov 23, 2026 report, had said gas production at the Khor Mor field was expected to resume in the coming days after a Monday meeting of delegations from Erbil and Baghdad with the field's operator, Dana Gas; that, according to information acquired by The New Region, the outcome of the meeting was positive, with Dana Gas set to resume gas production in the next two to three days; and that a source at the field told The New Region that all employees at Khor Mor had returned to work, that Dana Gas was set to release a statement on the resumption of operations in the near future, that efforts to repair the damaged sections were also expected to begin soon, and that production was expected to resume within the next 48 hours in areas unaffected by the attack. Omed Ahmed, spokesperson for the Kurdistan Region's electricity ministry, told The New Region on Monday that electricity generation at power stations was expected to resume within hours of gas production restarting, with supply gradually increasing, but that it could take up to 24 hours of normal operations for electricity production to return to pre-attack levels. Those earlier reports did not say that Khor Mor production or pre-attack electricity supply had already resumed. Kurdistan24, in a Nov 22, 2026 report, said the Nov 8 drone attack in Sulaimani province caused a large fire and stopped gas production entirely, with no casualties, and that the stoppage cut 2,500 to 2,800 megawatts of electricity in the Kurdistan Region and reduced power-supply hours by five to six hours a day. That account is consistent with earlier official figures: Al Jazeera, on Nov 9, citing Iraqi and Kurdish officials and the official Iraqi News Agency, said the attack left more than 70 percent of the Kurdish region without power and, citing Omed Ahmed, that it suspended gas supply to power plants in Erbil, Sulaymaniyah, Bazian, Chamchamal, and Duhok and knocked between 2,500 and 2,800 megawatts off the grid. Rudaw later quoted Ahmed as saying authorities had increased generation from approximately 1,000 megawatts immediately after the attack to 1,550 megawatts, of which 50 megawatts were reserved for essential facilities and factories, leaving 1,500 megawatts for residents and raising daily public electricity supply to six to eight hours; Ahmed said the electricity then available covered only 40 percent of demand, leaving a 60 percent shortfall, and that no date had been established for production to resume. Rudaw's article image assets for that report are dated Nov 13, 2026. 964media, in a Nov 15 report, quoted Ahmed as saying that no timeframe had been set for supplies to return to normal and that within 48 hours of the attack generation had been increased from 1,000 megawatts to nearly 1,650 megawatts. Dana Gas, in a Nov 14 clarification later restated in coverage including a Kurdistan24 report, said the facility had sustained significant damage and that no gas could currently be produced. The Insight International, in a Nov 21 report citing private-generator officials who spoke to Rudaw on Saturday, Nov 21, said the public grid remained weak because of the gas shortfall and that neighborhood generators were still running for most of the day in Erbil, Sulaimani, and Duhok. No official customer count was given. No official confirmation that Khor Mor production had already resumed was found as of 6:00 PM CT Friday, Nov 27 (3:00 a.m. Saturday, Nov 28, Iraq time).
outages.etr: No official firm restoration time was given. 964media, in a report dated 11:18 p.m. Friday, Nov 27, 2026, citing an unnamed technical source familiar with restart work, said the field was expected to return to operation on Sunday, Nov 29, 2026, at the KM250 section only, at 250 million cubic feet a day, about one-third of previous capacity, and that repairing the attacked KM400 section would take at least four to five months if work on it began; the same source said electricity supply in the Kurdistan Region could rise to about 12 hours a day if the entire 250 million cubic feet were allocated to the region, which the source said was not yet decided. That was an unnamed source's expectation, not an official Dana Gas or electricity-ministry timetable, and the report did not say production had already resumed. The New Region, in a Nov 23, 2026 report, said Dana Gas was set to resume gas production in the next two to three days after a positive Monday meeting, that a source at the field said production was expected to resume within the next 48 hours in areas unaffected by the attack, and that Omed Ahmed, spokesperson for the Kurdistan Region's electricity ministry, said electricity generation at power stations was expected to resume within hours of gas production restarting, though it could take up to 24 hours of normal operations to return to pre-attack electricity-production levels. No official confirmation that production had already resumed, and no official nationwide or Kurdistan-wide customer count or official firm restoration timetable, was found as of 6:00 PM CT Friday, Nov 27 (3:00 a.m. Saturday, Nov 28, Iraq time).
outages.updated: Nov 27, 2026, 964media dated 11:18 p.m. Friday, Nov 27 (= 2:18 p.m. CT if Iraq time), citing an unnamed technical source, on an expected Sunday, Nov 29, restart of the undamaged KM250 section at 250 million cubic feet a day, about one-third of previous capacity, on a four-to-five-month repair estimate for the attacked KM400 section, and on a possible rise to about 12 hours of electricity a day in the Kurdistan Region if that gas were allocated entirely to the region; the same report did not say production had already resumed and was not an official Dana Gas or electricity-ministry confirmation; earlier The New Region dated Nov 23, 2026, on a Monday meeting after which Dana Gas was described as set to resume production in the next two to three days; rechecked 6:00 PM CT Friday, Nov 27 (3:00 a.m. Saturday, Nov 28, Iraq time), no official confirmation that Khor Mor gas production had already resumed was found, and no official nationwide or Kurdistan-wide customer count or official firm restoration timetable was found

outages.place: Donetsk, Makiivka, Mariupol, Yenakiieve, Snizhne, Torez, Horlivka, and nearby districts, including Kirovskyi, Yasynuvata, Volodarske, Amvrosiivka, and Ilovaisk
outages.cause: Attacks on energy infrastructure, including a massive attack on the night of Nov 22, 2026, according to occupation officials, who said attacks on energy facilities were repeated the following night and that new outages were added to the effects of earlier damage. Occupation officials also described a power deficit and forced temporary outages to prevent accidents. On Thursday morning, Nov 26, the occupation Ministry of Coal and Energy, as reported by DNR News, said a large volume of emergency restoration work had been carried out over the previous day and that by morning almost the entire territory was supplied with electricity, while some local outages and forced temporary outages because of a shortage of available capacity continued. Later Thursday morning, occupation Donetsk administration head Alexei Kulemzin, citing Donetskenergo, said 507 transformer substations had been partially de-energized in all districts of Donetsk because the permissible load on the network had been exceeded. On Thursday evening, Kulemzin, again citing Donetskenergo as of 7:00 p.m. Thursday, said 556 transformer substations were partially de-energized in all districts of Donetsk for the same stated reason. Later Thursday evening, Kulemzin, again citing Donetskenergo, as published by Lenta novostei Donetska at 10:30 p.m. Thursday, Nov 26, said 518 transformer substations were partially de-energized in all districts of Donetsk because the permissible load on the network had been exceeded. On Friday evening, Nov 27, Kulemzin, again citing Donetskenergo, as published by Lenta novostei DNR at 7:11 p.m. Friday, said 324 transformer substations were partially de-energized in the Budennovsky, Kalininsky, Kievsky, Kirovsky, Petrovsky, Proletarsky, and Leninsky districts because the permissible load on the network had been exceeded.
outages.affected: Occupation Donetsk administration head Alexei Kulemzin, as published by Lenta novostei DNR at 7:11 p.m. Friday, Nov 27 (10:11 a.m. CT if Moscow time), citing Donetskenergo, a branch of JSC Yugo-Zapadnaya ESK, said that because the permissible load on the network had been exceeded, 324 transformer substations were partially de-energized in the Budennovsky, Kalininsky, Kievsky, Kirovsky, Petrovsky, Proletarsky, and Leninsky districts, and that 45,315 subscribers remained without electricity, with work under way to restore electricity supply. That Friday evening figure was higher than Friday morning's figures from the same official. Kulemzin, as published by Lenta novostei Donetska at 10:02 a.m. Friday, Nov 27 (1:02 a.m. CT if Moscow time), citing Donetskenergo, had said that 295 transformer substations were partially de-energized in the Kalininsky, Kievsky, and Proletarsky districts, and that 40,500 subscribers remained without electricity, with work under way to restore electricity supply. Kulemzin, as published by Lenta novostei Donetska at 10:30 p.m. Thursday, Nov 26 (1:30 p.m. CT if Moscow time), citing Donetskenergo, had said that 518 transformer substations were partially de-energized in all districts of Donetsk, and that 44,230 subscribers remained without electricity. Earlier Thursday, Kulemzin, as reported by Ostro at 6:45 p.m. Thursday, Nov 26, and by DNR News at 7:08 p.m. Thursday, citing Donetskenergo as of 7:00 p.m. Thursday (10:00 a.m. CT if Moscow time), had said 556 transformer substations were partially de-energized in all districts of Donetsk and that 57,848 subscribers remained without electricity. KP.ru, in a report dated 7:00 a.m. Friday, Nov 27, citing the occupation Ministry of Coal and Energy, said a tense situation remained in the region's energy system, that emergency restoration work was under way in Mariupol and the Novoazovsk municipal district, with energy workers hoping to finish repairs to damaged power lines by midday, that local outages were still being recorded in some districts of Donetsk, Makiivka, Horlivka, Dokuchaievsk, Yenakiieve, Snizhne, and Kirovske, and in the Yasynuvata, Amvrosiivka, and Shakhtarsk districts, and that as of Friday morning forced temporary outages because of a shortage of available capacity were in effect in the Donetsk urban district, the Amvrosiivka and Shakhtarsk districts, and Snizhne, and could spread to other municipalities during the day, with the time and duration of those outages impossible to name in advance. Earlier Thursday morning accounts from the occupation Ministry of Coal and Energy and Kulemzin, as previously recorded, had described a still-difficult situation in the region's energy system and remaining local and forced outages.
outages.start: Night of Sunday, Nov 22, 2026, local time, for the attack described by occupation officials; occupation officials said attacks on energy facilities were repeated the following night; a further failure at about 11:00 p.m. Monday, Nov 23, was reported on Tuesday morning; other partial outages in the region were already being reported
outages.etr: No official firm restoration time was given for the remaining outages. Occupation Donetsk administration head Alexei Kulemzin, as published by Lenta novostei DNR at 7:11 p.m. Friday, Nov 27, citing Donetskenergo, said work to restore electricity supply was under way and did not give a restoration time. Earlier, Kulemzin, as published by Lenta novostei Donetska at 10:02 a.m. Friday, Nov 27, and at 7:06 p.m. Thursday, Nov 26, citing Donetskenergo, likewise said work to restore electricity supply was under way and did not give a restoration time. KP.ru, in a report dated 7:00 a.m. Friday, Nov 27, citing the occupation Ministry of Coal and Energy, said energy workers hoped to finish repairs to damaged power lines in Mariupol and the Novoazovsk municipal district by midday Friday; that was a hope for those repairs, not a firm restoration time for the remaining outages. DNR News, citing the occupation Ministry of Coal and Energy at 9:14 a.m. Thursday, Nov 26, said forced temporary outages continued in some districts because of a shortage of available capacity, and that the time and duration of those outages could not be determined in advance because decisions were made operationally based on the current load. An earlier Sunday statement by occupation government head Andrei Chertkov, as reported by DNR News at 5:45 p.m. Sunday, Nov 22, had said restoration of the damaged energy center would take roughly two to three weeks.
outages.updated: Nov 27, 2026, occupation Donetsk administration head Alexei Kulemzin via Lenta novostei DNR 7:11 p.m. Friday, Nov 27 (= 10:11 a.m. CT if Moscow time), citing Donetskenergo, on 324 transformer substations partially de-energized in seven Donetsk districts and 45,315 subscribers remaining without electricity; earlier Kulemzin via Lenta novostei Donetska 10:02 a.m. Friday (= 1:02 a.m. CT if Moscow time), on 295 substations and 40,500 subscribers in three districts; KP.ru 7:00 a.m. Friday, citing the occupation Ministry of Coal and Energy, on remaining local and forced outages; earlier Thursday Kulemzin figures of 44,230 and 57,848 subscribers; rechecked 6:00 PM CT Friday, Nov 27 (3:00 a.m. Saturday, Nov 28, if Moscow time), no later official occupation update after the 7:11 p.m. Friday account, and no later official customer count, was found

outages.place: Crimea, including Sevastopol, Yalta, Feodosia, Yevpatoria, Saky, Armyansk, Dzhankoy, and Bilohirsk, and Nyzhnohirskyi, Saky, Sovietskyi, Chornomorskyi, Krasnoperekopsk, Bakhchysarai, Kirovskyi, Rozdolne, Pervomaiskyi, Krasnohvardiiske, and Simferopol districts
outages.cause: A further power outage in Crimea and Sevastopol on the afternoon of Thursday, Nov 26, 2026, which Krymenergo and Sevastopolenergo, as reported by RIA Novosti, attributed to an accident at energy facilities outside the peninsula. That afternoon outage came during an already announced restriction regime that occupation sources had attributed to a power-capacity shortage after strikes on transmission networks outside the peninsula, and to emergency repair work cited by occupation authorities as the reason for temporary supply restrictions beginning Wednesday, Nov 25. Krymskaya Gazeta, in a report dated 9:02 a.m. Thursday, Nov 26, citing Krymenergo, had said restrictions on the electric-power consumption regime had been introduced in the Republic of Crimea on Thursday, Nov 26, on the command of the federal System Operator, with an approximate outage duration of 3 to 12 hours. Sergei Aksenov, the occupation head of Crimea, had said Tuesday that beginning Wednesday, for a period of no more than 10 days, electricity supply would be restricted, with a planned 30 percent reduction in capacity from 8:00 a.m. to 9:00 p.m. and the peak of outages from 12:00 p.m. to 3:00 p.m., and that there would be no restrictions from 9:00 p.m. to 8:00 a.m.; RIA Novosti said those hours were Moscow time.
outages.affected: Sevastopolenergo, in a post on its official MAX channel, said the temporary electricity-supply restriction regime had been lifted, that the dispatcher of the Black Sea regional dispatch office (ChRDU) had given the command to connect all consumers until the next command to introduce restrictions, and that at 1:00 a.m. Saturday, Nov 28, 2026 (4:00 p.m. CT Friday, Nov 27), electricity supply to all consumers had been restored. That statement referred to the temporary restriction regime in Sevastopol and did not say that scheduled or later restrictions elsewhere on the peninsula had ended. Kommersant, in a report dated 8:13 p.m. Friday, Nov 27 (11:13 a.m. CT if Moscow time), citing Sevastopolenergo, had said that on Saturday, Nov 28, electricity supply for legal entities in Sevastopol would be limited from 5:00 a.m. to 12:00 a.m. because of emergency repair work on energy-system facilities outside the city, and that the company also asked ordinary consumers to reduce load on the network if possible. The occupation Ministry of Fuel and Energy of the Republic of Crimea, as published by Lenta novostei Kryma at 3:59 p.m. Friday, Nov 27 (6:59 a.m. CT if Moscow time), reported on restoration work after an accident on trunk networks on Nov 26, 2026, and on plans to normalize electricity supply on the peninsula. The same account said technical work was under way both at generation facilities and at high-voltage network facilities, that technical measures were also being carried out on the peninsula, and that the work was calculated to last until the end of the following week. It said available supply was being provided first to socially significant facilities, including health-care institutions, administrative buildings, and boiler houses, that because planned technical work was being carried out, restriction schedules had been adjusted and the period without electricity for consumers had been increased, and that additional outage schedules had been drawn up in each Krymenergo structural subdivision. The same account said restrictions on electricity deliveries had been temporarily strengthened because restoration work was continuing, that this was a forced measure, and that the restrictions introduced from Nov 25 were to be lifted by the end of the following week, by which time the necessary technical repair work was planned to be completed, after which consumers would return to regulated schedules and electricity supply would then be fully normalized. Ukrinform, in a report dated 10:53 a.m. Friday, Nov 27 (2:53 a.m. CT), citing Suspilne Crimea citing Krymenergo and Sevastopolenergo, said electricity was again being cut in Crimea after Thursday's blackout, that a temporary restriction regime had been introduced in Sevastopol because of necessary emergency work on federal networks outside the region, and that tram service in Yevpatoria had stopped and later resumed. No official customer count for Crimea or Sevastopol was found as of 6:00 PM CT Friday, Nov 27 (3:00 a.m. Saturday, Nov 28, if Moscow time).
outages.start: Occupation sources said peninsula-wide interruptions began Oct 24, 2026; the 10-day restriction regime described by occupation officials began Wednesday, Nov 25, 2026, with Rossiyskaya Gazeta saying the restrictions began to apply at 6:50 a.m. Wednesday. A further peninsula-wide outage on the afternoon of Thursday, Nov 26, 2026, was reported by Krymenergo and Sevastopolenergo, as published by RIA Novosti at 2:32 p.m. Thursday, Nov 26 (5:32 a.m. CT if Moscow time); those statements did not give a more precise official start time.
outages.etr: Sevastopolenergo, in a post on its official MAX channel, said that at 1:00 a.m. Saturday, Nov 28, 2026, electricity supply to all consumers in Sevastopol had been restored, until the next command to introduce restrictions. Kommersant, in a report dated 8:13 p.m. Friday, Nov 27, citing Sevastopolenergo, had said restrictions for legal entities in Sevastopol would apply on Saturday, Nov 28, from 5:00 a.m. to 12:00 a.m. The occupation Ministry of Fuel and Energy of the Republic of Crimea, as published by Lenta novostei Kryma at 3:59 p.m. Friday, Nov 27, said the restrictions introduced from Nov 25 were to be lifted by the end of the following week, by which time the necessary technical repair work was planned to be completed, after which consumers would return to regulated schedules and electricity supply would then be fully normalized; that was a stated plan for the peninsula-wide restriction regime, not a confirmation that supply on the peninsula had already been fully restored. Krymenergo, as reported by RIA Novosti Crimea on Wednesday morning, had said the approximate period of the restrictions introduced from Nov 25 was up to 10 days.
outages.updated: Nov 27, 2026, Sevastopolenergo via its official MAX channel, on the temporary restriction regime being lifted and on electricity supply to all consumers being restored at 1:00 a.m. Saturday, Nov 28 (= 4:00 p.m. CT Friday, Nov 27), until the next command to introduce restrictions; Kommersant 8:13 p.m. Friday, Nov 27 (= 11:13 a.m. CT if Moscow time), citing Sevastopolenergo, on Saturday legal-entity restrictions in Sevastopol from 5:00 a.m. to 12:00 a.m.; occupation Ministry of Fuel and Energy of the Republic of Crimea via Lenta novostei Kryma 3:59 p.m. Friday (= 6:59 a.m. CT if Moscow time), on restoration work after the Nov 26 trunk-network accident, on restrictions temporarily strengthened, and on a plan to lift the restrictions introduced from Nov 25 by the end of the following week; Ukrinform 10:53 a.m. Friday, citing Suspilne Crimea citing Krymenergo and Sevastopolenergo, on electricity again being cut in Crimea after Thursday's blackout; earlier Krymenergo and Sevastopolenergo via RIA Novosti 2:32 p.m. Thursday, Nov 26, on the Thursday afternoon peninsula-wide outage; rechecked 6:00 PM CT Friday, Nov 27 (3:00 a.m. Saturday, Nov 28, if Moscow time), no official customer count found

outages.cause: Generation-capacity deficit in the national electric system. CiberCuba, in a report dated Friday, Nov 27, describing the official UNE Friday bulletin, said unit 1 of CTE Santa Cruz and unit 2 of CTE Felton remained in breakdown, and that unit 3 of CTE Santa Cruz, unit 5 of CTE Nuevitas, unit 1 of CTE Felton, and unit 5 of CTE Renté remained in maintenance, a picture it said was practically identical to that of the rest of the week, and that thermal-generation limitations amounted to 494 MW. The same account said Thursday's solar photovoltaic parks produced 3,393 MWh, with a maximum of 528 MW, and that solar generation does not cover the deficit in the evening peak period, when demand is highest.
outages.affected: CiberCuba, in a report dated 10:32 a.m. Friday, Nov 27, and in its Nov 27 daily outage summary, described the official UNE Friday bulletin as forecasting 1,630 MW of affectation during the peak-demand period. According to those accounts of the official Friday report, availability of the SEN at 6:00 a.m. Cuba time Friday, Nov 27 (5:00 a.m. CT), was 1,075 MW, demand was 2,100 MW, and 1,035 MW were already without service at that hour. For the evening peak, UNE estimated availability of 1,100 MW against demand of 2,700 MW, a deficit of 1,600 MW, and a forecast affectation of 1,630 MW. CiberCuba said that peak-affectation forecast was about 45 MW, or about 2.7 percent, lower than the previous day's forecast of 1,675 MW. The same Friday accounts said the official report recorded the previous day's (Thursday, Nov 26) peak affectation as 1,689 MW at 6:40 p.m. Cuba time (5:40 p.m. CT), and that UNE estimated a midday Friday affectation of 1,300 MW. CiberCuba's Nov 27 daily summary also cited the Empresa Eléctrica de La Habana on Friday local circuit affectations and restorations in the capital from a generation-capacity deficit, including named midday interruptions and restorations, and said the Guantánamo electric company reported 38 MW of affectation and 25 MW served. No official national customer count was found as of 6:00 PM CT Friday, Nov 27 (7:00 p.m. Friday, Nov 27, Cuba time).
outages.updated: Nov 27, 2026, official UNE Friday bulletin as reported by CiberCuba dated 10:32 a.m. Friday, Nov 27, and by CiberCuba's Nov 27 daily outage summary, on Friday 6:00 a.m. Cuba time figures of 1,075 MW available, 2,100 MW demand, and 1,035 MW already without service, a midday affectation estimated at 1,300 MW, and a peak forecast of 1,100 MW available, 2,700 MW demand, a 1,600 MW deficit, and 1,630 MW of affectation; the same accounts on Thursday's recorded peak affectation of 1,689 MW at 6:40 p.m. Cuba time Thursday, Nov 26, and on unit 1 of CTE Santa Cruz and unit 2 of CTE Felton remaining in breakdown, with four other units in maintenance and thermal-generation limitations of 494 MW; Empresa Eléctrica de La Habana via CiberCuba's Nov 27 daily summary, on Friday local circuit affectations and restorations in Havana; rechecked 6:00 PM CT Friday, Nov 27 (7:00 p.m. Friday, Nov 27, Cuba time), no official national customer count found

outages.place: Sandakan, Tawau, Lahad Datu, Semporna, Kunak, Beluran, Telupid, and Kinabatangan
outages.cause: A collapse of a 275kV transmission tower in Ranau early Thursday morning, Nov 26, 2026, which Sabah Electricity said affected the west-to-east-coast transmission grid. The collapse of tower T313, detected at 6:04 a.m. Thursday, severed two transmission circuits linking Sabah's west and east coasts, according to Sabah Electricity, as reported by The Star, Malay Mail, H Metro, and Sinar Daily. Sabah Electricity's chief executive officer, Datuk Mohd Yaakob Jaafar, as reported by The Star at 8:48 p.m. Thursday, Nov 26, Malaysia time, said the tower's foundation along the banks of the Liwagu River was washed away following persistent heavy rains, resulting in the collapse of the tower, which is part of the grid that transmits 295 megawatts of electricity to the east coast. After the collapse, east-coast supply has been coming from existing generation in Sandakan and Tawau, supported by mobile generators and a battery energy storage system, with rotational load shedding because that local capacity is not enough to meet demand, according to Sabah Electricity accounts reported Friday by H Metro, The Star, and Sinar Daily.
outages.affected: Sabah Electricity, as reported by The Star at 7:55 p.m. Friday, Nov 27, Malaysia time (5:55 a.m. CT Friday), said it had completed the first phase of erecting a temporary Emergency Restoration System (ERS) tower in Ranau at 6:28 p.m. Friday (4:28 a.m. CT Friday), that its technical team would proceed with the second phase to restore the west-to-east-coast transmission link, that anchoring supports for the temporary tower had also been completed, and that despite light rain at the site the team was prioritizing safety. The same report, and Bernama in a report dated 6:52 p.m. Friday, Nov 27, Malaysia time (4:52 a.m. CT Friday), citing a Sabah Electricity Facebook video update, said that as of 3:00 p.m. Friday, Nov 27, Malaysia time (1:00 a.m. CT Friday), power-supply restoration in several east-coast districts had reached between 23 and 57 percent: Beluran 57 percent, Tawau 56 percent, Semporna 50 percent, Sandakan 45 percent, Kinabatangan 36 percent, Kunak 33 percent, and Lahad Datu 23 percent. Those accounts said restoration was being carried out through the Sandakan and Tawau power stations and a battery energy storage system (BESS), and that rotational load shedding was still required in some areas because available supply capacity could not yet meet current demand. The Star, in an earlier report dated 4:24 p.m. Friday, Nov 27, Malaysia time (2:24 a.m. CT Friday), said that under a rotational power-supply schedule released at 2:00 p.m. Friday, affected areas across seven districts — Sandakan, Tawau, Lahad Datu, Semporna, Kinabatangan, Beluran, and Kunak — had been divided into four groups, with rotations scheduled up to Monday, Nov 30, that each rotation was expected to receive electricity for three hours, and that the first rotation was to begin at 3:00 p.m. Friday, with actual timing and duration subject to grid conditions. The Thursday collapse, detected at 6:04 a.m., disrupted electricity supply across eight districts and affected 153,599 registered consumers, according to Sabah Electricity, as reported by The Star, Bernama, and Malay Mail.
outages.start: 6:04 a.m. Thursday, Nov 26, 2026, Malaysia time (4:04 p.m. CT Wednesday, Nov 25), according to Sabah Electricity, as reported by The Star, Malay Mail, and Sinar Harian
outages.etr: Sabah Electricity, as reported by The Star at 7:55 p.m. Friday, Nov 27, Malaysia time (5:55 a.m. CT Friday), said it was targeting full restoration of the electricity supply by Dec 3 at the latest. Bernama, in a report dated 6:52 p.m. Friday, likewise said the company expects to fully restore power by Dec 2, if not sooner. Sabah Electricity, as reported earlier by The Star at 4:24 p.m. Friday, Malaysia time (2:24 a.m. CT Friday), said a rotational power-supply schedule released at 2:00 p.m. Friday divided affected areas across seven districts into four groups, with rotations scheduled up to Monday, Nov 30, and that each rotation was expected to receive electricity for three hours, with actual timing and duration subject to grid conditions. The same earlier report said Sabah Electricity chairman Datuk Saadiah Aziz, at a press conference on Thursday night, said the company was targeting Dec 2 for full grid restoration. Those dates were stated targets, not an already completed restoration. Earlier, Sabah Electricity Chief Executive Officer Datuk Mohd Yaakob Jaafar, as reported by The Star at 8:48 p.m. Thursday, Nov 26, Malaysia time (6:48 a.m. CT Thursday), said they expect to restore normal power supply to 153,000 consumers latest by Dec 3, that they aim to restore the first transmission line on Dec 1 and both lines on Dec 2, but that because of conditions on the site they expect it to be fully restored by Dec 3.
outages.updated: Nov 27, 2026, Sabah Electricity via The Star 7:55 p.m. Friday, Nov 27, Malaysia time (= 5:55 a.m. CT Friday), on completion of the first phase of a temporary ERS tower in Ranau at 6:28 p.m. Friday, with the second phase to follow, and on a target of full restoration by Dec 3 at the latest; Sabah Electricity via Bernama 6:52 p.m. Friday (= 4:52 a.m. CT Friday) and via The Star, on restoration as of 3:00 p.m. Friday, Nov 27, Malaysia time (= 1:00 a.m. CT Friday), of Beluran 57 percent, Tawau 56 percent, Semporna 50 percent, Sandakan 45 percent, Kinabatangan 36 percent, Kunak 33 percent, and Lahad Datu 23 percent, with rotational load shedding continuing; The Star 4:24 p.m. Friday (= 2:24 a.m. CT Friday), on a four-group, three-hour rotational schedule through Nov 30; the Thursday collapse, detected at 6:04 a.m., affected 153,599 registered consumers across eight districts; rechecked 6:00 PM CT Friday, Nov 27 (8:00 a.m. Saturday, Nov 28, Malaysia time), no later official restoration-percentage update after the 3:00 p.m. Friday figures and no later official change to the Dec 2 or Dec 3 restoration targets found

outages.cause: Planned electricity restrictions that Tavanir said began Sunday, Nov 22, 2026, because fuel shortages were disrupting power generation
outages.affected: The Washington Post, in a report dated Nov 26, 2026, and marked 5:00 a.m. EST (4:00 a.m. CT), said Iran is rationing electricity and scaling back government subsidies on bread and gasoline. Al Jazeera, in a Nov 25, 2026 feature, said Iran was rationing electricity and described scheduled power cuts that officials had announced this week because fuel shortages were disrupting generation. Nour News, in a report published at 3:35 p.m. Tuesday, 3 Azar 1405 (6:05 a.m. CT Tuesday, Nov 24, if Iran time), on Wednesday, Nov 25 (4 Azar 1405) outages in Tehran, said a review of available notices found no confirmed public timetable that specified outage hours for all Tehran neighborhoods, and that customers should check the status of their subscription in the Bargh Man system, because timing could differ by area and subscription. The National, in an article dated November 23, 2026, and marked updated at 5:00 a.m., said scheduled cuts had begun and quoted Tavanir CEO Mohammad Allahdad as saying the restrictions may take the form of a two-hour outage over two days, or a maximum of two hours each day if temperatures fall, and quoted President Masoud Pezeshkian, via Isna, on expected winter difficulties. Euronews Persian, in a report dated 7:42 a.m. GMT+1 Monday, Nov 23 (12:42 a.m. CT Monday), said planned electricity outages began on Sunday, Nov 22 (1 Azar 1405), that Tavanir had announced the cuts on Saturday because of fuel-supply limitations at power plants, and that electricity-industry officials in Khorasan Razavi, Qazvin, and Kermanshah had confirmed the start of the restrictions. The same Euronews report, citing Mashhad distribution-company spokesman Majid Hassan-Nejad, said each outage turn in Mashhad would last two hours, though it was not yet clear whether the restrictions would be applied daily or with a gap of several days; citing Qazvin distribution-company official Seyed Mohammad Ghaflabashi, that household and commercial customers there were subject to the restrictions; and, citing Mehr news agency and Kermanshah distribution-company CEO Seyed Hamed Hosseini, that two-hour outages in Kermanshah were being applied between 9:00 a.m. and 6:00 p.m. Iran International, in a report dated 1:17 p.m. GMT Sunday, Nov 22 (7:17 a.m. CT), said scheduled cuts were resuming and that Sunday reports from Tehran, Isfahan, Shiraz, Mashhad, Yazd, Kermanshah, and Ardabil described hours-long outages, often without notice, and quoted Allahdad on restrictions beginning Nov 22 because of fuel shortages. Nour News, in a report dated 8:09 a.m. Iran time Sunday, Nov 22, or 1 Azar 1405 (10:39 p.m. CT Saturday), and Eghtesad Online, in a report dated 8:29 a.m. Iran time Sunday (10:59 p.m. CT Saturday) that cited Nour News, said planned electricity restrictions began that day and, citing the Tavanir chief executive, that the new restrictions may take the form of a two-hour outage over two days, or a maximum of two hours each day, that the timing is not fixed and may change with network conditions, and that customers would be informed through the Bargh-e Man system and app, the Bale messenger app, and text messages. Tavanir had announced on Saturday, Nov 21, that planned electricity restrictions on households and businesses would begin on Sunday, Nov 22, because fuel shortages were disrupting power generation, according to Iran International in a report dated 5:11 p.m. GMT Saturday, Nov 21 (11:11 a.m. CT), and to RFE/RL. Anar News, in a report updated at 12:05 a.m. UTC Sunday, Nov 22 (6:05 p.m. CT Saturday), citing BBC Persian, also said planned power outages began in Iran on Sunday, Nov 22, because of fuel shortages at power plants. A review of available Thursday, Nov 26 (5 Azar 1405), public notices found no confirmed official Tavanir nationwide timetable that listed Thursday outage hours for all regions or for all Tehran neighborhoods; earlier Nour News reporting had similarly said customers should check the Bargh Man system because timing could differ by area and subscription. No official nationwide customer count was found as of 12:00 PM CT Thursday, Nov 26 (9:30 p.m. Thursday, Nov 26, Iran time). Rechecked 6:00 PM CT Friday, Nov 27 (3:30 a.m. Saturday, Nov 28, Iran time), no official nationwide Tavanir timetable of Friday outage hours for all regions, no official nationwide customer count, and no official announcement that the planned restrictions that Tavanir said would begin Sunday, Nov 22, had ended, was found.

outages.cause: Drone attacks on power stations and other electricity infrastructure during the war between the Rapid Support Forces and the Sudanese Armed Forces
outages.affected: No official customer count. Al Jazeera, in a report dated Nov 27, 2026, last updated at 2:10 p.m. Makkah time (5:10 a.m. CT Friday), described continuing electricity interruptions in Omdurman, west of Khartoum, that were delaying work at leather workshops and other small businesses, and said that over two weeks 15 electricity transformer stations in Gedaref, Khartoum, Gezira, Red Sea, Sennar, White Nile, South Kordofan, Blue Nile, River Nile, and Northern states had been attacked and heavily damaged, causing power cuts in a number of cities. The same report referred to accounts from earlier in November that the Rapid Support Forces had continued to bomb Sudanese electricity and fuel stations with drones. Drop Site News, in a Nov 20, 2026 report from Khartoum, said a particularly intense wave of drone strikes at the end of October and into November targeting power stations, fuel supplies, and electricity infrastructure had brought the country's power grid to the brink of collapse, and that two weeks after the wave of attacks, major substations remained out of service. Shaker Ismail, an engineer with the Sudanese Electricity Company, told Drop Site that repairing some of the country's most important power facilities could take months or longer, that high-capacity transformers and digital control systems had been damaged, and that replacement transformers must be manufactured to order abroad. Ismail said the Um Dabakir thermal power plant in White Nile State was badly damaged in an Oct 29 strike and forced to shut down, and that the Al-Markhiyat substation west of Omdurman was put out of service after an Oct 27 strike. Rechecked 6:00 PM CT Friday, Nov 27 (2:00 a.m. Saturday, Nov 28, Sudan time), no official national customer count or official restoration timetable was found.
